prompt: 60 backlog items remain on a client's MVP. Weekly throughput over the last six weeks was 6, 9, 7, 8, 5 and 10 items.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.

fields.label: Weeks to finish at the average
Weeks to finish at the slowest week's rate

task.explanation: Average = 45/6 = 7.5. 60/7.5 = 8 weeks. At the slowest (5/week) 60/5 = 12 weeks: a useful pessimistic bound.

prompt: A Monte Carlo simulation of 1,000 runs for the remaining work produced these completion results. Read the forecast off the cumulative counts.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.

fields.label: Week by which at least 50% of runs finish
Week by which at least 85% of runs finish

task.explanation: Cumulative: wk8 = 300, wk9 = 620, wk10 = 820, wk11 = 940, wk12 = 1000. 50% (500) is first reached at week 9; 85% (850) at week 11.

prompt: The team splits epics into stories as they go. Historically each remaining epic becomes 1.5× as many items as first listed. There are 40 items listed now and throughput averages 8 items a week.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.
task.explanation: 40 × 1.5 = 60 items; 60 / 8 = 7.5 weeks. Ignoring split/growth is the most common cause of optimistic forecasts.

prompt: A PM's forecast email to a client. Mark the statements that are poor forecasting practice.

task.prompt: Mark every segment that is a problem. Leave the sound ones unmarked.

segments.text: Based on the last 8 weeks of throughput, we forecast completion between 14 and 18 June.
There's an 85% likelihood we finish by 18 June.
This is a guaranteed date; nothing can change it.
segments.issue: Forecasts are probabilistic; presenting one as a guarantee sets up a broken promise.

segments.text: The forecast assumes the remaining scope stays at about 45 items.
We'll update the forecast every week as new data comes in.
We based it on the single fastest week we've ever had, so it's achievable.
segments.issue: Using the best week ignores variability; use the distribution of throughput instead.

prompt: Order these steps for producing a throughput-based Monte Carlo forecast.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: Read completion dates at chosen percentiles (50%, 85%)
Count the remaining items (adjusted for expected splitting)
Collect recent weekly throughput (e.g. last 8–12 weeks)
Simulate many futures by randomly sampling past weekly throughputs until the items are done
Share a range with confidence levels and refresh it regularly

task.explanation: Data, scope, simulation, percentiles, then communicate and refresh.

prompt: A client's CEO asks: 'When will the white-label app be done? I need one date for the board.' Your Monte Carlo gives 50% by 3 March and 85% by 24 March.

task.prompt: A client's CEO asks: 'When will the white-label app be done? I need one date for the board.' Your Monte Carlo gives 50% by 3 March and 85% by 24 March.

steps.question: Which date do you give for a board commitment?
options: 3 March, it's more attractive
24 March, stating it's the 85% confidence date
A date before 3 March to impress
No date at all
steps.explanation: A public commitment needs high confidence; explain the percentile so the board understands the risk.

steps.question: The CEO says the board needs 3 March. What do you offer?
options: Promise 3 March and hope
Options: reduce scope to what fits by 3 March at 85% confidence, or accept 50% odds knowingly
Ask the team for overtime without telling anyone
Refuse to discuss
steps.explanation: Show the trade-off between scope and confidence rather than overpromising.

steps.question: Two weeks later, scope grows by 15 items. What do you do?
options: Keep the old forecast
Re-run the forecast with the new scope and communicate the new dates promptly
Remove the items from Jira
Wait until the end to mention it
steps.explanation: Forecasts are refreshed with new data; prompt updates preserve trust.

prompt: What does an '85% forecast of 24 March' mean?

options: In 85% of simulated outcomes the work finished on or before 24 March
85% of the work will be done on 24 March
The team works at 85% speed
The date is 85% of the way through the project
mcq.explanation: A percentile forecast gives the share of possible outcomes that finish by that date.

prompt: Why do flow-based forecasts use throughput (item counts) rather than adding up story points?

options: Item counts need no estimating and, with similarly sized items, forecast about as well using real delivery data
Story points are banned in Kanban
Throughput is always higher
Clients prefer counts
mcq.explanation: Counting finished items uses actual data, avoids estimation effort, and works when items are right-sized.

prompt: Your forecast data comes from a period when the team had 6 developers; next quarter it will have 4. What should you do?

options: Treat the old throughput as unrepresentative: adjust or rebuild the forecast as new data arrives, and widen the range meanwhile
Use the old data unchanged
Multiply throughput by 6/4
Stop forecasting
mcq.explanation: Monte Carlo assumes the future resembles the sampled past; when the system changes, the data must be adjusted and the uncertainty acknowledged.
